title: Lengths and ratios
blurb: Power of a point, radical axes, the ratio lemma with Ceva and Menelaus, and mass points, for AIME computation and BMO proofs.
outcomes: Use signed power of a point, radical axes and radical centres in proofs and computations
Turn angle data into side ratios with the ratio lemma and trig Ceva
Read off ratios and areas in cevian configurations with mass points
lesson:
If three circles meet in pairs, the three lines containing their common chords pass through one point. There is no useful angle to chase in this figure, and the proof below uses the power of a point instead. This unit covers the methods based on lengths and ratios: power of a point, radical axes, the ratio lemma with Ceva and Menelaus, and mass points. They are the standard methods for AIME geometry and for BMO1 problems about lengths.

Power of a point

Theorem. Let $\omega$ have centre $O$ and radius $r$, and let $P$ be any point. If a line through $P$ meets $\omega$ at $A$ and $B$, then \[\overline{PA}\cdot\overline{PB}=OP^2-r^2,\] where bars denote signed lengths along the line, so the product is negative exactly when $P$ is inside the circle. The number $\operatorname{pow}(P)=OP^2-r^2$ is the power of $P$. If $PT$ is a tangent, $PT^2=\operatorname{pow}(P)$.

Proof: let $M$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $O$ to the line, which is the midpoint of $AB$. With signed lengths, $\overline{PA}\cdot\overline{PB}=(\overline{PM}+\overline{MA})(\overline{PM}-\overline{MA})=PM^2-MA^2=(OP^2-OM^2)-(OA^2-OM^2)=OP^2-r^2$. The tangent is the case $A=B=T$.

The converse is used just as often. If lines $AB$ and $CD$ meet at $P$ and $\overline{PA}\cdot\overline{PB}=\overline{PC}\cdot\overline{PD}$, then $A,B,C,D$ are concyclic: line $PC$ meets circle $ABC$ again at a point $D'$ with $\overline{PC}\cdot\overline{PD'}=\overline{PA}\cdot\overline{PB}$, so $D'=D$. Likewise, $PT^2=\overline{PA}\cdot\overline{PB}$ makes $PT$ tangent to circle $ABT$.

Radical axis and radical centre

Radical axis. For two circles with different centres, the points with equal power with respect to both form a line perpendicular to the line of centres. If the circles meet at $X$ and $Y$, it is line $XY$; if they touch, it is the common tangent at the point of contact.

Radical centre. For three circles with non-collinear centres, the three radical axes meet at one point.

Put the centres at $(0,0)$ and $(d,0)$. The condition $x^2+y^2-r_1^2=(x-d)^2+y^2-r_2^2$ simplifies to $x=\dfrac{d^2+r_1^2-r_2^2}{2d}$, a line perpendicular to the line of centres, and common points of the circles (power $0$ for both) lie on it. For three circles, two of the axes are perpendicular to non-parallel lines, so they meet at a point $R$; then $R$ has the same power for all three circles, so it lies on the third axis. This proves the statement at the start of the unit.

In practice, a point on the common chord line has equal tangents to both circles; four points are concyclic when two lines through them meet at a point with equal products; three lines are concurrent when they are radical axes of three circles.

The ratio lemma, Ceva and Menelaus

Ratio lemma. If $D$ lies on side $BC$ of triangle $ABC$, then \[\frac{BD}{DC}=\frac{AB\,\sin\angle BAD}{AC\,\sin\angle DAC}.\]

Ceva. For $D,E,F$ on sides $BC,CA,AB$, the lines $AD,BE,CF$ are concurrent if and only if $\dfrac{BD}{DC}\cdot\dfrac{CE}{EA}\cdot\dfrac{AF}{FB}=1$. In trigonometric form, if and only if $\dfrac{\sin\angle BAD}{\sin\angle DAC}\cdot\dfrac{\sin\angle CBE}{\sin\angle EBA}\cdot\dfrac{\sin\angle ACF}{\sin\angle FCB}=1$.

Menelaus. If a line meets lines $BC,CA,AB$ at $D,E,F$, the same product of unsigned ratios equals $1$; conversely, if the product is $1$ and one or three of the points lie outside the sides, the points are collinear.

The ratio lemma is an area comparison: triangles $ABD$ and $ADC$ share the height from $A$, so $\dfrac{BD}{DC}=\dfrac{[ABD]}{[ADC]}=\dfrac{\frac12 AB\cdot AD\sin\angle BAD}{\frac12 AC\cdot AD\sin\angle DAC}$. The angle bisector theorem is the special case of equal angles. For Ceva, if the cevians meet at $P$ then $BD/DC=[ABP]/[ACP]$ (subtract the two pairs of triangles with bases $BD$, $DC$), and the three such ratios multiply to $1$; the converse follows because the ratio determines the point. Trig Ceva follows from Ceva by applying the ratio lemma three times, since the side lengths cancel. Use the ratio lemma whenever you know angles at a vertex and want a ratio on the opposite side, or the reverse.

Mass points

Mass points record the ratios in a Ceva configuration. Put masses $m_A,m_B,m_C>0$ at the vertices. The centre of mass of $B$ and $C$ is the point $D$ of $BC$ with $BD:DC=m_C:m_B$ (the lever law: the heavier mass is nearer), and it carries mass $m_B+m_C$. The centre of mass $P=\dfrac{m_AA+m_BB+m_CC}{m_A+m_B+m_C}$ of all three is also the centre of mass of $A$ and $D$, so $P$ lies on $AD$ with $AP:PD=(m_B+m_C):m_A$. Similarly, grouping the masses differently shows $P$ is on the other two cevians as well. Moreover $[PBC]:[PCA]:[PAB]=m_A:m_B:m_C$. So once the masses match two given ratios, every other ratio and area in the figure can be read off.

Worked examples

Example 1. Circles $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$ meet at $X$ and $Y$. A common tangent, nearer to $X$ than to $Y$, touches $\omega_1$ at $A$ and $\omega_2$ at $B$. Given $AB=24$ and $XY=10$, find the distance from $X$ to the midpoint of $AB$.

Neither radius is known, so coordinates are awkward. The circles are related through their common chord, which lies on their radical axis, so we use powers. Let line $XY$ meet $AB$ at $M$. Since $M$ is on the radical axis, $MA^2=MX\cdot MY=MB^2$, so $M$ is the midpoint of $AB$ and $MA=12$.

The tangent line lies outside both circles, so $M$ has positive power and $X$, $Y$ are on the same side of $M$, with $X$ nearer. Hence, writing $MX=x$, we get $x(x+10)=144$, so $(x-8)(x+18)=0$ and $x=8$.

Example 2. In triangle $ABC$, the circle through $A$ tangent to $BC$ at $B$ meets line $AC$ again at $P$, and the circle through $A$ tangent to $BC$ at $C$ meets line $AB$ again at $Q$. Prove that the circumcentre of triangle $APQ$ is equidistant from $B$ and $C$.

You met this configuration in L4-GE1, where angles produced a fixed point. Angle chasing gives many equal angles but nothing about the circumcentre $Z$. Instead, if $\rho$ is the radius of circle $APQ$, then $ZB^2-\rho^2$ and $ZC^2-\rho^2$ are the powers of $B$ and $C$. So it suffices to show that $B$ and $C$ have equal power with respect to circle $APQ$.

$B$ lies on line $AQ$, so its power is $\overline{BQ}\cdot\overline{BA}$. But $Q$ and $A$ also lie on the circle tangent to $BC$ at $C$, and $BC$ is a tangent from $B$ to that circle, so $\overline{BQ}\cdot\overline{BA}=BC^2$. In the same way the power of $C$ is $\overline{CP}\cdot\overline{CA}=CB^2$. The powers are equal, and it follows that $ZB=ZC$. Because the lengths are signed, no case analysis is needed: wherever $P$ and $Q$ fall on their lines, the products are the powers.

Example 3. In triangle $ABC$ of area $21$, $AB=6$ and $AC=9$. The bisector of angle $A$ meets $BC$ at $D$, the median from $B$ meets $AC$ at its midpoint $M$, and $AD$ meets $BM$ at $P$. Line $CP$ meets $AB$ at $F$. Find $AP:PD$, $BP:PM$, $AF:FB$ and the area of triangle $APB$.

Coordinates would work but are slow, and $BC$ is not given. The data are ratios on two sides, so we use mass points. By the angle bisector theorem $BD:DC=6:9=2:3$, so we need $m_C:m_B=2:3$; take $m_B=3$, $m_C=2$. As $M$ is the midpoint of $AC$, $m_A=m_C=2$.

Then $AP:PD=(m_B+m_C):m_A=5:2$, $BP:PM=(m_A+m_C):m_B=4:3$ and $AF:FB=m_B:m_A=3:2$. For the area, $[APB]:[ABC]=m_C:(m_A+m_B+m_C)=2:7$, so $[APB]=6$. Check with Ceva: $\frac23\cdot 1\cdot\frac32=1$. A common error is to put $BD:DC=m_B:m_C$, which is the wrong way round.

Example 4. Triangle $ABC$ has $AB=6$, $AC=8$, $BC=7$. The tangent to its circumcircle at $A$ meets line $BC$ at $T$. (a) Find $TA$. (b) Prove that every point $X$ on the circle $\Gamma$ with centre $T$ through $A$ satisfies $XB:XC=3:4$.

(a) One could find angles with the cosine rule, but the tangent gives a similarity directly. Since $AB<AC$ we have $\angle C<\angle B$, and the tangent at $A$ meets line $BC$ beyond $B$. By the alternate segment theorem $\angle TAB=\angle ACB$, and triangles $TAB$, $TCA$ share the angle at $T$, so they are similar and \[\frac{TA}{TC}=\frac{TB}{TA}=\frac{AB}{CA}=\frac34.\] Thus $TB=\frac{9}{16}TC$ and $TC-TB=7$. This gives $TC=16$, $TB=9$, and $TA=12$; indeed $TA^2=144=TB\cdot TC$.

(b) For $X$ on $\Gamma$ but not on line $BC$, $TX^2=TA^2=TB\cdot TC$, so by the converse of power of a point $TX$ is tangent to circle $XBC$. Exactly as in (a), $\triangle TXB\sim\triangle TCX$, so $XB:XC=TX:TC=12:16=3:4$. The two points of $\Gamma$ on line $BC$ are $L$ with $BL=3$, $LC=4$, and $L'$ with $L'B=21$, $L'C=28$, which also fit.

So $\Gamma$ is the Apollonius circle of the ratio $3:4$. Note that $L$ is the foot of the bisector from $A$, so $TA=TL$, a fact often used in AIME problems.

Common traps.

  • Forgetting signs: inside the circle, $PA\cdot PB=r^2-OP^2$. Signed lengths handle every case at once.
  • Putting mass points backwards: $BD:DC=m_C:m_B$.
  • Applying Ceva to points on extensions, or Menelaus to points all on the sides, without care.
  • Ratio lemma with the wrong angles: they are the angles at $A$, not at $D$.
  • In AIME computations, keeping the wrong root of a quadratic or the wrong configuration (is $T$ beyond $B$ or beyond $C$?).

How to spot this in a contest

The usual signals are as follows.

  1. Products of lengths along lines through one point: power of a point.
  2. Two circles with a common chord or a common tangent: the radical axis. Three circles, or three lines that should be concurrent: the radical centre.
  3. A tangent at a vertex meeting the opposite side: the similarity $TAB\sim TCA$.
  4. Angles at a vertex together with a ratio on the opposite side: the ratio lemma or trig Ceva.
  5. Cevians with given ratios, or areas cut by cevians: mass points.

In AIME problems, compute in exact fractions and check the answer against a rough scale drawing.

practice.q: Circles $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$ have radii $13$ and $15$, and their centres are $14$ apart. A point $P$ on the line through their two common points is at distance $20$ from the line of centres. Find the length of a tangent from $P$ to $\omega_1$.
practice.hint: Locate the radical axis with the formula, then the power of $P$ is $O_1P^2-13^2$.
practice.sol:
Put $O_1=(0,0)$ and $O_2=(14,0)$. The radical axis is the line $x=\dfrac{14^2+13^2-15^2}{2\cdot 14}=5$, so $P=(5,20)$ (or its mirror image, which gives the same answer). The square of the tangent length is the power $O_1P^2-13^2=25+400-169=256$, so the tangent has length $16$.

As a check, the power with respect to $\omega_2$ is $9^2+20^2-15^2=256$ too, as it must be for a point on the radical axis.

practice.q: Triangle $ABC$ has area $120$. Point $D$ lies on $BC$ with $BD:DC=1:2$, and $E$ lies on $CA$ with $CE:EA=1:3$. The segments $AD$ and $BE$ meet at $P$. Find the area of quadrilateral $PDCE$.
practice.hint: Choose masses to match both ratios; the masses are proportional to the areas $[PBC]$, $[PCA]$, $[PAB]$.
practice.sol:
We need $m_C:m_B=BD:DC=1:2$ and $m_A:m_C=CE:EA=1:3$. Take $m_A=1$, $m_C=3$, $m_B=6$, with total $10$. Then $P$ is the centre of mass and $[PBC]:[PCA]:[PAB]=1:6:3$, so $[PBC]=12$ and $[PCA]=72$.

Triangles $PDC$ and $PBC$ share the height from $P$, so $[PDC]=\frac{DC}{BC}[PBC]=\frac23\cdot 12=8$. Similarly $[PCE]=\frac{CE}{CA}[PCA]=\frac14\cdot 72=18$. Hence $[PDCE]=8+18=26$.

practice.q: In triangle $ABC$, $AB=4$, $AC=6$ and $\angle BAC=120^\circ$. The point $D$ on $BC$ satisfies $\angle BAD=90^\circ$. Find $BD/DC$.
practice.hint: You know both angles at $A$ on either side of $AD$.
practice.sol: Since $\angle BAD=90^\circ$, $\angle DAC=120^\circ-90^\circ=30^\circ$. By the ratio lemma, \[\frac{BD}{DC}=\frac{AB\sin\angle BAD}{AC\sin\angle DAC}=\frac{4\cdot 1}{6\cdot\frac12}=\frac43.\] The length $BC$ was not needed.

practice.q: From a point $P$ outside a circle $\omega$ with centre $O$, the tangents touch $\omega$ at $A$ and $B$, and $M$ is the midpoint of $AB$. A line through $P$, not through $O$, meets $\omega$ at $C$ and $D$. Prove that $O$, $M$, $C$, $D$ are concyclic.
practice.hint: Express $PA^2$ in two ways: once with the circle, once with the right-angled triangle $PAO$.
practice.sol:
Since $PA=PB$ and $OA=OB$, both $P$ and $O$ lie on the perpendicular bisector of $AB$. So line $PO$ is that bisector, it passes through the midpoint $M$, and $AM\perp PO$. The radius $OA$ is perpendicular to the tangent $PA$, so triangle $PAO$ has a right angle at $A$, and $AM$ is its altitude. Triangles $PMA$ and $PAO$ are similar (they share the angle at $P$ and each has a right angle), giving $PM\cdot PO=PA^2$.

By power of a point, $PA^2=PC\cdot PD$. Therefore $PM\cdot PO=PC\cdot PD$. Here $M$ and $O$ lie on one ray from $P$, and $C$ and $D$ lie on another ray from $P$, since $P$ is outside the circle, so the equality holds for signed lengths as well. The two lines are different because the line $PCD$ does not pass through $O$. By the converse of power of a point, $O$, $M$, $C$, $D$ are concyclic. $\blacksquare$

practice.q: Triangle $ABC$ has $AB=13$, $BC=14$, $CA=15$. The circle with diameter $BC$ meets $AB$ again at $F$ and $AC$ again at $E$. Line $EF$ meets line $BC$ at $T$. Find $TB$.
practice.hint: Menelaus works. Alternatively, line $EF$ is the radical axis of the circle on diameter $BC$ and another circle through $E$ and $F$ that meets $BC$ at known points.
practice.sol:
The angles $\angle BFC$ and $\angle BEC$ are right, so $F$ and $E$ are the feet of the altitudes from $C$ and $B$. Let $D$ be the foot of the altitude from $A$ and $M$ the midpoint of $BC$; the familiar $13$-$14$-$15$ split gives $BD=5$, $DC=9$, and $BM=7$.

The nine-point circle passes through $D$, $E$, $F$, $M$, and the circle with diameter $BC$ passes through $B$, $C$, $E$, $F$. Their radical axis is line $EF$, so $T$ has equal powers: $\overline{TB}\cdot\overline{TC}=\overline{TD}\cdot\overline{TM}$. Since $E$ and $F$ lie on the sides, Menelaus says $T$ is outside segment $BC$, and $T$ is on the side of $B$ (checked below). With $TB=x$, \[x(x+14)=(x+5)(x+7),\] so $14x=12x+35$ and $x=\tfrac{35}{2}$.

Check by Menelaus: $BF=14\cos B=\frac{70}{13}$, $AF=\frac{99}{13}$, $CE=14\cos C=\frac{42}{5}$, $AE=\frac{33}{5}$, and $\frac{AF}{FB}\cdot\frac{BT}{TC}\cdot\frac{CE}{EA}=1$ gives $\frac{BT}{TC}=\frac{70}{99}\cdot\frac{33}{42}=\frac59$. So $TB<TC$, $T$ is beyond $B$, and $TC-TB=14$ gives $TB=\frac{35}{2}$ again.

practice.q: Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with $AB\neq AC$, orthocentre $H$, and let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$. The circle through $A$ tangent to $BC$ at $B$ and the circle through $A$ tangent to $BC$ at $C$ meet again at $K$. Prove that $K$ lies on $AM$ and that $HK\perp AM$.
practice.hint: For the first part, compare the powers of $M$. For the second, show $K$ is on circle $BHC$, and find a diameter of that circle with one end on line $AM$.
practice.sol:
Call the circles $\Gamma_B$ (tangent at $B$) and $\Gamma_C$ (tangent at $C$).

$K$ lies on $AM$. The power of $M$ with respect to $\Gamma_B$ is $MB^2$, since $MB$ is a tangent, and with respect to $\Gamma_C$ it is $MC^2$. As $MB=MC$, $M$ is on the radical axis of $\Gamma_B$ and $\Gamma_C$. So is $A$, a common point, and $A\neq M$, so the radical axis is line $AM$. The common point $K$ also lies on it, so $A$, $K$, $M$ are collinear. Moreover $\overline{MK}\cdot\overline{MA}=MB^2$. Since $\angle BAC$ is acute, $A$ lies outside the circle with diameter $BC$, so $MA>MB$; hence $0<MK<MA$ and $K$ lies on segment $MA$, with $K\neq A$.

$K$ lies on circle $BHC$. Use directed angles modulo $180^\circ$. The tangent criterion in $\Gamma_B$ gives $\measuredangle BKA=\measuredangle(BC,BA)$, and in $\Gamma_C$ gives $\measuredangle CKA=\measuredangle(CB,CA)$. Hence \[\measuredangle BKC=\measuredangle BKA-\measuredangle CKA=\measuredangle(BC,BA)+\measuredangle(CA,BC)=\measuredangle(CA,BA)=\measuredangle CAB.\] Since $HB\perp AC$ and $HC\perp AB$, turning both lines through $90^\circ$ gives $\measuredangle BHC=\measuredangle(AC,AB)=\measuredangle CAB$. So $\measuredangle BKC=\measuredangle BHC$ and $B,K,H,C$ are concyclic.

The right angle. Let $A'$ be the reflection of $A$ in $M$, so $ABA'C$ is a parallelogram. Then $BA'\parallel AC\perp BH$, so $\angle HBA'=90^\circ$, and likewise $\angle HCA'=90^\circ$. Hence $A'$ lies on circle $BHC$ and $HA'$ is a diameter. Now $K\neq A'$: otherwise $MK=MA$ and $MK\cdot MA=MB^2$ would give $MA=MB$, so $\angle BAC=90^\circ$, which is false. Also $K\neq H$, since $H$ on the median $AM$ would make the altitude and the median from $A$ coincide, forcing $AB=AC$. So $K$ is a point of the circle with diameter $HA'$ other than its ends, and $\angle HKA'=90^\circ$. As $K$ and $A'$ lie on line $AM$, $HK\perp AM$. $\blacksquare$
